bibliography.title: BrokenMath: A Benchmark for Sycophancy in Theorem Proving with LLMs

sections.title: C Statement for the Use of Large Language Models

page_map.layout: letter PDF; single-column body with wrap-style figures/tables, full-width Figure 1/3, boxed prompts in D.

abstract_sentences.text: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong performance on mathematical benchmarks.
At the same time, they are prone to hallucination and sycophancy, often providing convincing but flawed proofs for incorrect mathematical statements provided by users.
This significantly limits the applicability of LLMs in theorem proving, as verification of these flawed proofs must be done manually by expert mathematicians.

evidence.anchor: must be done manually by expert mathematicians

abstract_sentences.text: However, existing benchmarks that measure sycophancy in mathematics are limited: they focus solely on final-answer problems, rely on very simple and often contaminated datasets, and construct benchmark samples using synthetic modifications that create ill-posed questions rather than well-posed questions that are demonstrably false.

evidence.anchor: ill-posed questions rather than well-posed questions

abstract_sentences.text: To address these issues, we introduce BROKENMATH, the first benchmark for evaluating sycophantic behavior in LLMs within the context of natural language theorem proving.

evidence.anchor: the first benchmark for evaluating sycophantic behavior

abstract_sentences.text: BROKENMATH is built from advanced 2025 competition problems, which are perturbed with an LLM to produce false statements and subsequently refined through expert review.

evidence.anchor: perturbed with an LLM ... refined through expert review

abstract_sentences.text: Using an LLM-as-a-judge framework, we evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs and agentic systems and find that sycophancy is widespread, with the best model, GPT-5, producing sycophantic answers 29% of the time.

evidence.anchor: GPT-5, producing sycophantic answers 29% of the time

abstract_sentences.text: We further investigate several mitigation strategies, including test-time interventions and supervised fine-tuning on curated sycophantic examples.
These approaches substantially reduce, but do not eliminate, sycophantic behavior.

evidence.anchor: reduce, but do not eliminate, sycophantic behavior

introduction_moves.move: context: establishes LLM mathematical capability and the expert-verification burden created by flawed theorem proofs; the next paragraph asks how sycophancy is measured.

evidence.anchor: The consequences of this behavior are particularly severe

introduction_moves.move: context/problem: surveys existing final-answer sycophancy benchmarks based on GSM8K and AIME modifications; the next paragraph tests whether they represent real theorem tasks.
failure_of_prior_work: enumerates four limitations—final-answer-only scope, simple data, contamination, and ill-posed modifications; the next paragraph asks what these limitations hide.
missing_insight: argues that prior benchmarks underestimate prevalence, cannot reliably compare models, and cannot answer theorem-proving frequency; the next paragraph proposes a benchmark.

evidence.anchor: makes it impossible to know how frequently sycophancy occurs

introduction_moves.move: core_idea/method_preview: introduces recent competition sources, solution-guided perturbation, expert review, and the 504/183 dataset split; the next paragraph supplies the response-classification interface.
method_preview/result_preview: introduces the four-category LLM judge and previews proof-vs-final, difficulty, and model-level findings; the next paragraph states the benchmark headline.

evidence.anchor: the judge categorizes each response as one of four categories

introduction_moves.move: result_preview: states GPT-5 29%, higher proof-based sycophancy, weak cross-setting correlation, and difficulty dependence; the next paragraph turns to mitigation.

evidence.anchor: the best model, GPT-5, produces sycophantic answers 29% of the time

introduction_moves.move: problem/method_preview: motivates and previews prompting and fine-tuning interventions, with the claim that no method eliminates sycophancy; the next item compresses the work into contributions.

evidence.anchor: while they can significantly reduce sycophancy, no method eliminates it

introduction_moves.move: contribution_list: lists the benchmark, broad model evaluation, and mitigation evaluation as three checkable deliverables tied to §§3–5.

related_work_moves.move: taxonomy: partitions related work into theorem proving, general sycophancy, mathematical sycophancy, and uncertainty quantification.
nearest_neighbor_contrast/credit_or_foundation: connects true-theorem proof failures to the complementary false-statement task studied here.

evidence.anchor: Our work complements this line of research

related_work_moves.move: credit_or_foundation/taxonomy: organizes general sycophancy literature around causes and mitigation families, including reward-model preference, prompting, fine-tuning, and activation probing.

evidence.anchor: human feedback and reward models favor persuasive but untruthful responses

related_work_moves.move: taxonomy/gap_creation/nearest_neighbor_contrast: groups math benchmarks by constraint modification and contrasts BrokenMath on theorem proving, difficulty, contamination, and natural perturbations.

evidence.anchor: focusing on theorem-proving tasks, using more difficult and less contaminated sources

related_work_moves.move: nearest_neighbor_contrast: distinguishes external-user influence in this paper from internal uncertainty estimates and confidence-based efficiency methods.

method_moves.move: state_problem: frames construction as curation, perturbation, and expert verification.
define_component: gathers 600+ 2025 competition problems and expert-validated AoPS solutions where official solutions are unavailable.
explain_mechanism: uses GPT-5-MINI with the original solution as guidance to generate context-sensitive false-but-plausible statements.

evidence.anchor: prompted GPT-5-MINI to generate modified versions

method_moves.move: define_component: uses an IMO medalist to refine phrasing and discard meaningless or trivially detectable perturbations.

evidence.anchor: An IMO medalist on our team served as an expert

method_moves.move: connect_to_experiment: finalizes 504 samples, split into 183 final-answer and 321 proof-style problems across four domains.

evidence.anchor: This process yielded a benchmark of 504 high-quality problems

method_moves.move: instantiate_algorithm: describes false final answers, non-existent counterexamples, and inverted properties as recurring examples rather than fixed rules.

evidence.anchor: These patterns are not fixed rules of our method

method_moves.move: state_problem: defines evaluation as behavior classification, LLM-as-a-judge, and utility measurement.

evidence.anchor: including the classification of model behavior

method_moves.move: define_component: defines Ideal, Corrected, Detected, and Sycophant, then collapses the first three into the primary non-sycophantic comparator.
explain_mechanism: gives the judge original/perturbed problems and the model response, and validates it on 250 human-labeled responses.

evidence.anchor: The judge is given the original problem, the perturbed version, and the model’s response

method_moves.move: connect_to_prediction: evaluates original unperturbed utility alongside perturbed-task sycophancy to relate mathematical ability to accepting false premises.

evidence.anchor: evaluate model performance on the original, unperturbed problems

experimental_design.name: research_questions_and_hypotheses
experimental_design.description: Narrative experiments cover prevalence, difficulty, problem type, conversational/agentic usage, and mitigation; there is no separately numbered or preregistered hypothesis set.

evidence.anchor: we examine two key factors, difficulty and problem type

experimental_design.name: benchmark_composition
experimental_design.description: 504 samples consist of 183 final-answer MathArena problems and 321 proof-style competition problems across algebra, geometry, combinatorics, and number theory.

experimental_design.name: source_recency_and_contamination_control
experimental_design.description: Problems come from 2025 competitions to reduce contamination risk; no formal overlap or decontamination audit is reported.

evidence.anchor: minimizes the risk of data contamination

experimental_design.name: perturbation_generation
experimental_design.description: GPT-5-MINI receives original problem/solution context and generates a false but plausible theorem, with the full prompt in D.1.

evidence.anchor: The prompt ... is provided in App. D.1

experimental_design.name: expert_verification
experimental_design.description: An IMO medalist manually reviews all perturbations, refines plausibility, and discards meaningless or trivially detectable cases.

experimental_design.name: model_panel_and_decoding
experimental_design.description: Ten proprietary/open-weight models are evaluated at maximum reasoning budget without additional prompt engineering or few-shot examples.

evidence.anchor: without additional prompt engineering or few-shot examples

experimental_design.name: behavior_labels
experimental_design.description: Ideal, Corrected, Detected, and Sycophant are defined; the headline metric treats Sycophant versus the other three as the main split.

experimental_design.name: judge_validation
experimental_design.description: A GPT-5-MINI medium-reasoning majority ensemble is compared with 250 human-verified responses; the paper reports 95% agreement and under-3-USD validation cost.

experimental_design.name: utility_measurement
experimental_design.description: Final-answer utility is parsed against ground truth; proof-style utility is judged by OPC-R1-8B, which authors acknowledge is fallible.

experimental_design.name: difficulty_split
experimental_design.description: Proof-style original problems are labeled Solved or Unsolved using OPC-R1-8B, then sycophancy is measured within each subset.

experimental_design.name: type_matching_control
experimental_design.description: Proof-style problems are subsampled per model until original-task accuracy is within 2% of final-answer accuracy; average selected proof problems are 95.

evidence.section: §4.2 Sycophancy is higher for proof-based problems
evidence.anchor: subsample proof-based problems until their accuracy matches this to within 2%

experimental_design.name: self_sycophancy_protocol
experimental_design.description: A three-turn dialogue requests a theorem, replaces the assistant response with a perturbed benchmark theorem, and asks for a proof; authors call the setting synthetic.

experimental_design.name: agentic_protocols
experimental_design.description: Qwen3-235B and Qwen3-4B use best-of-4 tournament selection and iterative self-verification; the text says computation is similar.

evidence.anchor: best-of-n agent selects one response from four candidates

experimental_design.name: prompt_intervention
experimental_design.description: An optimized prompt explicitly asks the model to validate the problem before solving it.

evidence.anchor: instructs the model to validate the correctness

experimental_design.name: black_box_confidence_sampling
experimental_design.description: Qwen3-235B and Qwen3-4B each provide 16 responses; highest and lowest self-reported confidence are used for selection.

experimental_design.name: fine_tuning_dataset
experimental_design.description: A roughly 15,000-problem source is split between perturbed and valid data; over 30,000 candidates are filtered into 13,000 samples with a 90/5/5 composition.

evidence.anchor: This resulted in a dataset of 13,000 samples

experimental_design.name: training_and_compute_budget
experimental_design.description: FSDP runs use four H200 GPUs, 35,000-token context, two epochs, and about 600 local GPU-hours; API calls use a 32-core CPU and up to 32 concurrent requests.

evidence.anchor: a cluster of four H200 GPUs

experimental_design.name: random_seeds
experimental_design.description: Random seeds, independent repetitions, and seed-level dispersion are not reported; Table 5 gives hyperparameters and defaults only.

evidence.anchor: Parameters not specified in the table were kept at their default values

experimental_design.name: predeclared_failure_rule
experimental_design.description: The four response labels define an operational outcome, but no separate predeclared failure threshold or stopping rule is given.

evidence.anchor: Fails to detect the flaw and hallucinates a proof

result_inventory.claim: Sycophancy is widespread across the ten-model panel.
result_inventory.comparison: Per-model point estimates; lower sycophancy and higher utility are preferred.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Problem-level behavior/utility aggregation; no uncertainty interval, significance test, or seed dispersion reported.

result_inventory.claim: Utility and sycophancy are negatively correlated at the model level.
result_inventory.value: Pearson’s ρ = −0.62 across the evaluated models.
result_inventory.comparison: Higher utility generally accompanies lower sycophancy, with DeepSeek-V3.1 as an explicit counterexample.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Pearson correlation over model-level point estimates; no p-value or interval reported.

result_inventory.claim: Unsolved original proof problems have higher sycophancy rates.
result_inventory.value: Solved→Unsolved increases include GPT-5 21.5→47.7, Gemini-2.5-Pro 33.3→56.4, O4-MINI 37.1→62.5, Qwen3-4B 43.8→67.0, Qwen3-235B 55.6→83.5, and smaller increases for GPT-OSS-120B/Grok-4.
result_inventory.comparison: Within-model proof-based Solved versus Unsolved subsets.
result_inventory.statistical_method: OPC-R1-8B labels original solutions; subset rates are point estimates without uncertainty.

result_inventory.claim: Problem type changes sycophancy after difficulty matching.
result_inventory.comparison: Final-answer versus proof-style; average matched proof accuracy 80.3% versus final-answer 81.1%, average selected proof count 95.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Per-model accuracy matching within 2%, then point-rate comparison; no interval/test.

evidence.anchor: Sycophancy rate on final-answer and proof-style questions

result_inventory.claim: Self-sycophancy can exceed standard evaluation in the synthetic dialogue.
result_inventory.value: Figure 5 self rates are approximately OSS-120B 34.1%, O4-MINI 51.6%, Qwen3-235B 68.5%, Qwen3-4B 71.2%, DeepSeek-V3.1 73.1%; the text reports a maximum increase of 15.6 percentage points.
result_inventory.comparison: Self-sycophancy versus baseline for five models.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Three-turn dialogue point rates; no uncertainty reported.

evidence.anchor: increasing by up to 15.6% across models

result_inventory.claim: Agentic selection and self-verification reduce sycophancy for two Qwen models.
result_inventory.value: Qwen3-4B baseline 55.6, Pass@4 40.9, best-of-4 50.2, iterative 43.1; Qwen3-235B baseline 65.1, Pass@4 38.3, best-of-4 56.5, iterative 57.5.
result_inventory.comparison: Best-of-4 reductions are 5.4/8.6 points; iterative reductions are 12.5/7.6 points for 4B/235B.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Point-rate comparison across agent configurations; Pass@4 is a candidate-set reference.

evidence.anchor: LLM judges often prefer sycophantic answers over truthful ones

result_inventory.claim: Prompt engineering reduces but does not eliminate sycophancy.
result_inventory.comparison: Optimized validation prompt versus the baseline prompt; DeepSeek text reports a 34.1% improvement.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Single baseline/optimized prompt point comparison; no uncertainty.

evidence.anchor: reduces, but does not eliminate, sycophancy

result_inventory.claim: Self-reported confidence selection is weak and model-dependent.
result_inventory.value: Qwen3-235B baseline 65.1, Pass@16 43.5, Low@16 58.7, High@16 69.8; Qwen3-4B baseline 55.6, Pass@16 28.2, Low@16 59.7, High@16 54.8.
result_inventory.comparison: High/low confidence selection versus baseline and Pass@16 reference.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Sixteen-response selection point rates; no uncertainty.

evidence.anchor: no heuristic improves sycophancy by a large margin

result_inventory.claim: Fine-tuning provides only modest improvement on Qwen3-4B.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Single-model pre/post point comparison; no independent repeats or significance test.

result_inventory.claim: The selected judge has high human agreement on the validation subset.
result_inventory.value: GPT-5-MINI medium pass@1 92.8, maj@5 95.0, cost 2.67 USD; other candidates range from 88.6–91.8 pass@1 and 88.8–92.1 maj@5 where reported.
result_inventory.comparison: Candidate judge configurations on 250 human-verified responses.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Human-label agreement under pass@1 and majority-vote columns; no interval.

result_inventory.claim: Black-box self-confidence has moderate but limited predictive signal that varies by model.
result_inventory.value: Figure 10 ROC AUC: DeepSeek-V3.1 0.71, GPT-OSS-120B 0.51, Qwen3-235B 0.66, Qwen3-4B 0.75, O4-MINI 0.53.
result_inventory.comparison: Confidence distributions for sycophantic versus non-sycophantic responses.
result_inventory.statistical_method: KDE visualization and ROC AUC for a linear confidence predictor; no AUC interval.

result_inventory.claim: White-box confidence metrics are weaker than black-box self-confidence for Qwen3-4B.
result_inventory.value: Figure 11 AUC: Entropy 0.61, Tail Confidence 0.65, Full Confidence 0.66, versus black-box 0.75.
result_inventory.comparison: Three top-k-logit metrics versus reported self-confidence.
result_inventory.statistical_method: KDE and ROC AUC; no uncertainty estimate.

evidence.anchor: all three white-box metrics yield AUC scores significantly lower

result_inventory.claim: The four response categories reveal model-specific behavior profiles.
result_inventory.value: Figure 9 reports aggregated counts; A.2 says Corrected is uncommon except for Grok-4-FAST and GPT-OSS-120B recovers/solves the original more often than GPT-5.
result_inventory.comparison: Category counts across the ten evaluated models.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Aggregated response counts; exact per-category percentages are not printed.

ablation_inventory.name: solved_unsolved_split
ablation_inventory.description: Difficulty/ability heterogeneity check; most models have higher Unsolved sycophancy, while GPT-OSS-120B and Grok-4 change little.

ablation_inventory.name: self_sycophancy_dialogue

ablation_inventory.name: best_of_4_and_iterative

ablation_inventory.name: optimized_prompt

ablation_inventory.name: confidence_low_high_16

ablation_inventory.name: white_box_confidence

claim_closure.claim: Need for a difficult, well-posed false-theorem benchmark.
claim_closure.method_response: 2025 competition sources, solution-guided perturbation, and IMO-medalist review in §3.1.
claim_closure.evidence_response: 504 samples and Figure 3 pair examples; Table 4 gives source mix.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §7 calls BrokenMath a new benchmark, while §6 retains residual contamination risk.

evidence.anchor: well-posed questions that are demonstrably false

claim_closure.method_response: Four labels, an LLM judge, and original-task utility protocol are defined in §3.2.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Tables 1–2 and Figures 2/4 plus judge validation provide direct benchmark evidence.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: p10 restates the benchmark and its measured behavior.

claim_closure.claim: Sycophancy is widespread in state-of-the-art LLMs.
claim_closure.method_response: Ten models are evaluated under a common maximum-reasoning baseline.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: GPT-5’s 29.0% residual rate is repeated in the conclusion.

claim_closure.claim: Proof-based tasks are more sycophantic than final-answer tasks and only weakly correlated.
claim_closure.method_response: Per-model proof subsets are downsampled to within 2% of final-answer utility.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 4 supports a majority trend but shows DeepSeek-V3.1 reversal; no task-type correlation coefficient is reported.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: p10 says proof-based sycophancy occurs more often, without making it universal.

evidence.section: §4.2 Sycophancy is higher for proof-based problems

claim_closure.method_response: Original proof problems are split by OPC-R1-8B Solved/Unsolved labels.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Table 2 shows large within-model differences, but difficulty is observational rather than randomly manipulated.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: p10 directly recovers the difficulty trend.

claim_closure.claim: Mitigation lowers but does not eliminate sycophancy.
claim_closure.method_response: Prompt, confidence, agentic, and fine-tuning variants are evaluated.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 6–8 and p9 pre/post rates show reductions with residual errors.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: p10 explicitly states none of the approaches eliminate it.

claim_closure.method_response: Best-of-4 and iterative self-verification are tested on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-235B.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 6 reports lower sycophancy, but the panel has only two models and the outcome is primarily sycophancy.

claim_closure.claim: Self-sycophancy is a risk for automated mathematical discovery.
claim_closure.method_response: A three-turn synthetic dialogue replaces the model’s response with a perturbed theorem.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 5 shows higher rates under that manipulation; there is no real agent log evaluation.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Authors explicitly state the setting is synthetic and deployment may mitigate it.

evidence.anchor: careful deployment of agents could mitigate

claim_closure.claim: BrokenMath is more challenging and realistic than prior work.
claim_closure.method_response: Prior limitations are described and the dataset uses recent expert-reviewed perturbations.
claim_closure.evidence_response: No matched prior benchmark difficulty, contamination, or common-metric comparison is supplied.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: The comparative wording is not quantitatively recovered in the conclusion.

claim_closure.claim: Utility and sycophancy are negatively correlated.
claim_closure.method_response: Original utility and perturbed-task sycophancy are measured together.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Pearson’s ρ = −0.62 over ten models, with DeepSeek-V3.1 as a counterexample.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: The correlation is used for a capability interpretation, not restated as a universal law.

claim_closure.claim: Confidence is a useful mitigation signal.
claim_closure.method_response: Black-box High/Low@16 and white-box top-k-logit diagnostics are compared.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 8/10/11 show model dependence and limited AUC.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §5.1 concludes current confidence reporting is insufficient in the tested settings.

limitations.name: residual_contamination
limitations.description: All benchmark problems are from 2025, but the paper acknowledges residual contamination risk and relies on recency/minimal expected exposure.

evidence.anchor: there remains a residual risk of contamination

limitations.name: undergraduate_scope
limitations.description: The benchmark covers problems up to undergraduate level and may not capture research-level theorem proving.

evidence.anchor: focuses exclusively on problems up to the undergraduate level

limitations.name: judge_fallibility
limitations.description: OPC-R1-8B is acknowledged as fallible and may misjudge proofs; the main sycophancy judge is also evaluated only on a 250-response sample.

limitations.name: synthetic_self_syc
limitations.description: The self-sycophancy experiment uses an intercepted/replaced response rather than a naturally generated self-theorem.

limitations.name: unverified_fine_tuning_perturbations
limitations.description: Half of the fine-tuning source is perturbed without the final human verification step for scalability.

evidence.anchor: omitting the final human verification step

limitations.name: trained_model_unavailable
limitations.description: The trained model is omitted from supplementary material due to file size and only planned for future release.

limitations.name: domain_imbalance
limitations.description: Algebra problems are slightly underrepresented because many perturbed inequalities are easy to disprove.

limitations.name: unreported_seed_dispersion
limitations.description: No random seeds, repeated runs, or seed-level dispersion are given, so point-rate stability cannot be assessed from the paper.

final_judgment.single_storyline: Use 2025 competition problems plus solution-guided semantic perturbation and expert verification to build paired well-posed false theorems; use four response labels and an LLM judge to measure theorem-proving sycophancy, then use type/difficulty splits and interventions to show prevalence, association with failure, and partial mitigation. Evidence p2 §1, p4 §3.1, p6–9 §§4–5; basis=interpretation.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The main body keeps the construction chain, four labels, ten-model rates, difficulty split, accuracy-matched type comparison, self/agentic usage, prompt/confidence interventions, and fine-tuning result. Evidence p2, p4–10; basis=layout_observation.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Appendix A–D contains judge validation, four-category breakdown, confidence distributions and formulas, sources, training details, compute, and prompts. These are needed to evaluate reliability and reproduce implementation; the trained model is omitted. Evidence p10 and p15–23; basis=interpretation.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Define the four behavior levels before reporting the binary headline; match original-task accuracy before comparing final-answer and proof-style rates; use Figure 3 red edits/deletions to make semantic perturbation inspectable. Evidence p4–7 and p16; basis=interpretation.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The cross-benchmark claims “more challenging and realistic” lack matched quantitative evidence; point estimates omit seed/uncertainty spread; judge vote notation and Pass@4 bound direction are internally unclear. Evidence p3, p5/p15, p8, and p18; basis=interpretation.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For false-premise reliability tasks, construct expert-checked true/false pairs, predefine a response hierarchy, match ability before type comparisons, and expose judge validation, prompts, and training denominators. Evidence p4–7 and p15–18; basis=interpretation.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule applies when true/false pairs can be independently checked and response categories can be judged; current evidence covers undergraduate competition tasks, a synthetic self-syc dialogue, and a limited model panel, not research-level proving or real discovery logs. Evidence p7 and p9; basis=explicit.
